items.item: Bytes solves a different problem than Cow: Cow defers a clone that might never happen; Bytes avoids ever needing to clone at all, by making the shared, refcounted handle the normal way to hold the data from the start

at.step: bytes::Bytes: owning the share, not borrowing it

items.item: A naive self-referencing struct fails for a structural reason, not an incidental one: Rust is free to move a struct's bytes to a new address at any point, and a reference baked in at construction time would then point at the old, no-longer-valid address

at.step: A struct that borrows its own field

items.item: ouroboros's generated builder doesn't bypass the moving problem, it works around it: the owning field is placed into its final storage first, and the borrowing field is only constructed afterward against that now-stable address, with the type keeping both fields pinned together behind accessor methods instead of direct field access

at.step: ouroboros makes the same shape safe

items.item: Yoke's framing of 'erasing a lifetime' is the same move as Box<dyn Trait> erasing a concrete type: in both cases a piece of compile-time information (a lifetime, a type) is replaced with a value that carries what it needs to stay valid at run time instead

at.step: Why yoke and ouroboros exist at all

items.item: Choosing among &'a [u8], Cow<'a, [u8]>, and an owned Vec<u8> is really a question of who needs to hold onto the data and for how long: a borrow for a call that returns before the source does, Cow for mostly-read data that might occasionally need a private copy, and an owned Vec when the data must genuinely outlive its source

at.step: Cow: borrowed until something needs to change

items.item: Network and async code reaches for Bytes specifically because a received buffer's lifetime is tied to the connection or task that received it, which a borrow usually cannot be tied to across an await point or a handed-off task boundary
